notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Numbers 11, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Numbers 11 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1

The opening is abrupt: literally, "the people were as complainers, evil in the ears of the LORD" (Pulpit Commentary). The Hebrew *kemithonenim* suggests they "made themselves impatient," working themselves into a restless, discontented, murmuring state—a half-suppressed fretting rather than open complaint (Pulpit, George Bush via Precept Austin). The Septuagint reads, "the people murmured sinfully before the Lord." Although no specific grievance is named, the Pulpit Commentary suggests the fatigue and anxiety of the march after a year's relative idleness at Sinai were the likely cause. David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes the contrast: Israel had been ordered, cleansed, blessed, and given God's presence in chapters 1–10; now, after only three days' march, they complain. The "fire of the LORD" may have been lightning (so Ellicott, Peake), a supernatural fire from the pillar, or a burning desert wind (Gill cites Thevenot's report of a 1658 wind that killed 20,000). The fire consumed "the outskirts of the camp"—a mercy, notes Guzik, since God might have cast fire into the very centre. Importantly, prior to Sinai God had tolerated such murmurings (Exodus 15–17); now, after the covenant, judgment came swiftly, because their responsibilities had grown with their privileges (Pulpit).

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-11-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm

### v. 2

The people cried out to Moses—not directly to God—because they lacked a personal sense of relationship with the LORD (Guzik). Moses acted as intercessor, a type of Christ the mediator (Gill). The fire "was quenched" or more precisely "sank down" (Hebrew *shāqaʿ*), as if it subsided into the earth. Gill notes this language fits the idea of a burning wind subsiding. No further detail is given on the extent of the destruction, but the intercession of Moses stopped it.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/11.htm

### v. 3

The place was named *Taberah*, meaning "burning." This is the first of several naming-narratives in the wilderness journey, memorialising divine judgment (Merrill, cited at Precept Austin). The Pulpit Commentary notes that Taberah does not appear in the list of stations in Numbers 33; it may have been a spot within the three-day march from Sinai, or identical with Kibroth-hattaavah (v. 34), though the narrative treats them separately.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-11-commentary
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm

### v. 4

The "rabble" (Hebrew *ha-saphsuph*, "the gathered"; BSB: "rabble") refers to the "mixed multitude" that came out of Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38)—non-Israelites, perhaps Egyptians and others, many possibly offspring of mixed marriages (Pulpit). They "yielded to intense craving" (Hebrew *taʾăvâ*), a word used for strong desire, often sinful (Guzik). Guzik stresses that they had to yield; temptation does not simply overtake us. The "mixed multitude" infected the Israelites: "evil communication corrupts good manners" (Gill, citing 1 Corinthians 15:33). Constable (StudyLight excerpt) notes that these malcontents despised God's provision of manna and longed for the stronger flavours of Egypt. G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik) said of them: "not having true part or lot in the Divine movement, they fell a-lusting after the things of Egypt, and infected the people of God with the same unholy desire."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-11.html

### vv. 5–6

Israel romanticised their past. The foods listed—fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic—were exactly the produce of the Nile delta (Cole, cited by Guzik). Classical writers attest that fish in the Nile cost next to nothing (Diodorus Siculus, Herodotus, cited by Pulpit). Gill notes the irony: they forgot how dearly they paid for that fish through hard bondage. Guzik calls this "selective memory"—choosing to recall one small, good aspect of slavery while ignoring the bitter bondage. The claim "our whole being is dried up" was a wild exaggeration; God had never let them go hungry. They complained not of lack of food but of lack of variety (Guzik). Pulpit adds that the words for cucumber, melon, and garlic were probably Egyptian loanwords, a mark of the narrative's authenticity.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm

### vv. 7–9

The manna is described: like coriander seed (small, round), in colour like bdellium (opalescent white—Pulpit; though Gill notes bdellium may mean a pearl or crystal). It was ground in hand-mills, beaten in mortars, boiled in pots, or made into cakes. It tasted like pastry prepared with oil (or honey, Exodus 16:31). It fell with the dew at night. The Pulpit Commentary observes that the description, far from being inserted simply to show the people's unreasonableness, might also acknowledge that a monotonous diet of manna for a year was a real trial to the palate—yet the sin was in despising God's provision, not in feeling the lack.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm

### v. 10

The weeping was public and orchestrated—"every man in the door of his tent"—designed to make a spectacle and pressure Moses (Pulpit). Both the LORD's anger and Moses' displeasure were aroused. The Pulpit Commentary observes that Moses sinned here by failing to distinguish between righteous indignation for God and angry impatience with men. His displeasure was understandable but not wholly righteous.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/

### vv. 11–15

Moses' complaint is raw and desperate. He asks why God has "afflicted" him and why he has not found favour—as if being called to lead was a curse. His rhetorical questions—"Did I conceive all these people? Did I give them birth?"—cast him as an unwilling mother. The Pulpit Commentary says these passionate complaints were "clearly wrong, because exaggerated": God had not laid on Moses the burden of providing flesh or single-handedly carrying the nation into Canaan. Moses forgot himself as mediator and "in his indignation at the sin of the people committed the same sin himself" (Pulpit). Guzik is gentler: Moses did the right thing in pouring out his heart to God, but his complaint showed a lapse in trust. His cry "kill me right now" echoes Elijah (1 Kings 19) and Jonah (Jonah 4), and God answered none of them with death but with renewed provision and purpose. John Piper (DesiringGod) applies this to pastoral ministry: spiritual leadership is hard, and congregations can drive their pastors to despair through chronic grumbling.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/kill-me-at-once

### vv. 16–17

God's response is gracious and practical. He does not rebuke Moses; he addresses the reasonable part of the complaint by appointing seventy elders to share the burden (Pulpit). The seventy were to be men already "known" as elders and officers—elders are made by God but recognised by men (Guzik). They were to stand with Moses at the Tent of Meeting, and God would take "some of the Spirit" (*rûaḥ*) that was on Moses and place it on them. The Pulpit Commentary notes this is distinct from the appointment of judges in Exodus 18 (Jethro's advice), which concerned secular administration; this concerns spiritual leadership and the gift of the Spirit. Peake's Commentary (StudyLight) observes that the Spirit is here regarded as "a quasi-physical fluid, capable of being divided and imparted to others"—a conception consistent with the early Old Testament period. Jewish tradition (Trapp, cited by Guzik) held that the Sanhedrin originated here. 

**Pentecostal/Charismatic note:** David Guzik (EnduringWord) emphasises that the elders received "the same Spirit" that rested on Moses so they could lead "with unity of vision." The impartation of the Spirit for leadership is seen as a foreshadowing of the Spirit's outpouring on all believers.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-11.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-11-commentary

### vv. 18–20

God promises meat—but as judgment, not blessing. The people must "consecrate" themselves (ironically, for a feast that would become their punishment). They would eat meat not for a day or two, but "a whole month—until it comes out of your nostrils and makes you nauseous." Guzik: "Sometimes God disciplines His people by giving them what they ask for." The key charge is in v. 20: "because you have rejected the LORD, who is among you." Their complaint about food was in reality a rejection of God Himself. Constable notes God kept them in that place for a full month, making the judgment protracted.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-11.html

### vv. 21–23

Moses expresses unbelief. He cites 600,000 foot-soldiers (implying a total population of perhaps 2 million) and asks whether slaughtering all their flocks or catching all the fish in the sea could feed them for a month. God's reply—"Is the LORD's arm too short?"—is a rebuke that recalls His power and points Moses away from human calculation to divine omnipotence. Guzik: "God's response reminds him that God's resources are inexhaustible and not dependent on human logic." The Pulpit Commentary notes Moses' unbelief is stark but recorded with honesty, a mark of the narrative's genuineness.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm

### vv. 24–25

Moses obeyed: he relayed God's words to the people and gathered the seventy around the Tent. The LORD came down in the cloud (the same cloud that led them) and placed the Spirit on the elders. They "prophesied"—likely ecstatic utterance (cf. 1 Samuel 10:10; 19:20–24)—"but they never did so again." This was a one-time sign authenticating their Spirit-endowed authority, not an ongoing prophetic ministry (Constable, Guzik). Gill notes the Spirit was "taken" from Moses—not diminishing what Moses had, but as one candle lights another without losing its own flame.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic note:** Guzik sees this event as foreshadowing the outpouring of the Spirit under the New Covenant. The fact that the Spirit "rested" on them and they prophesied is emphasised as a model of Spirit-empowered leadership.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-11.html

### vv. 26–29

Two men, Eldad and Medad, had remained in the camp—they were on the list of seventy but had not gone to the Tent—yet the Spirit rested on them and they prophesied in the camp. A young man reported it; Joshua (Moses' attendant "since youth") urged Moses to stop them. Moses' reply is one of the noblest in Scripture: "Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!" Guzik calls this a revelation of Moses' "selfless character" and a foreshadowing of the New Covenant outpouring (Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:17–18). Constable notes the central purpose of the narrative is to show "Moses longed for a much different type of community … guided by God's Spirit."

**Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis:** Guzik and EnduringWord highlight this verse as foundational for the belief that God desires all His people to experience the Spirit's empowering, not just a select few. The event at Pentecost (Acts 2) is seen as the fulfilment of Moses' wish.

**Reformed/Baptist note:** John Piper (DesiringGod) uses this passage less to emphasise Pentecostal experience and more to underscore Moses' humility and the principle that God distributes His Spirit sovereignly to whom He wills for the work of ministry.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-11.html
- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/lord-let-me-die

### v. 30

Moses and the elders returned to the camp—a simple transitional verse. The Pulpit Commentary has no separate note; the verse marks the return to ordinary life after the extraordinary events at the Tent.

### vv. 31–32

A wind "sent by the LORD" (*rûaḥ*—the same word for "Spirit" used earlier—Guzik) drove quail from the sea. They fell around the camp about two cubits (approximately three feet / one metre) above the ground, for a day's journey (about 20 miles) in every direction. The people gathered quail for about 36 hours straight. The smallest amount gathered was "ten homers"—a homer being roughly 6–8 bushels or 220 litres, making ten homers an absurdly large quantity (perhaps 60–80 bushels per person). Gill and Guzik note the greed: they spread the quail "all around the camp" to dry or cure the meat—they intended to stockpile it. The natural phenomenon of migratory quail blown off course is well-attested in the Sinai region, but the timing, quantity, and precise location were supernatural (Pulpit, Constable).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/11.htm

### v. 33

"While the meat was still between their teeth, before it was chewed"—a graphic image of judgment arriving at the very moment of gratification. The wrath of the LORD was aroused and He struck them with "a severe plague." Psalm 106:15 provides the theological commentary: "He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul" (KJV). Guzik: "Receiving our ungodly cravings can bring spiritual leanness and death." Constable calls it disciplinary, not vindictive—designed to teach the people to accept what God sends as best. Gill does not speculate on the medical nature of the plague; the text simply says God struck them.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-11.html

### v. 34

The place was named *Kibroth-hattaavah*, meaning "graves of the craving" or "graves of lust." Those who had "craved other food" (or "yielded to craving," echoing *taʾăvâ* from v. 4) were buried there. The naming memorialises the sin and its punishment together, as Taberah did earlier.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-11/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/11.htm

### v. 35

From Kibroth-hattaavah they moved to Hazeroth (meaning "enclosures"), where the events of Numbers 12 (Miriam and Aaron's rebellion) took place. Constable notes this was after their month-long stay at Kibroth-hattaavah.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-11.html

---

## Denominational Distinctives

The sources I could access do not reveal sharp confessional disagreements on Numbers 11. Differences are more a matter of emphasis:

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (EnduringWord / David Guzik): Strong emphasis on the Spirit being "placed" on the seventy elders and the prophecy that resulted. Moses' words in v. 29 ("I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets") are interpreted as a direct foreshadowing of Pentecost and the charismatic dimension of New Covenant life. The Spirit is highlighted as empowering for ministry, not merely for office.

- **Reformed/Baptist** (DesiringGod / John Piper): Emphasis falls on Moses' despair, the burden of spiritual leadership, and God's sovereign provision of help through shared leadership. The Spirit's distribution is treated as God's sovereign work, and the narrative's primary application is ecclesiological (shared leadership in the church) rather than charismatic.

- **Older commentators** (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit): These treat the passage historically and philologically, with careful attention to Hebrew wording and historical context. They do not press the passage toward distinctively charismatic or cessationist conclusions; the prophesying of the elders is understood as a one-time sign of office.

- **Methodist/Wesleyan and Lutheran sources** were not accessible in my searches for Numbers 11 specifically.

- **Catholic/Orthodox, modern scholarship, prosperity/word-of-faith** sources were not returned by my searches for this passage.

---

## Summary of the Chapter's Movement

1. **vv. 1–3**: General complaining punished by fire at Taberah; Moses intercedes.
2. **vv. 4–9**: The rabble incites craving for meat; Israel despises the manna; the manna is described.
3. **vv. 10–15**: Moses, overwhelmed, complains to God and asks for death.
4. **vv. 16–25**: God appoints seventy elders, places the Spirit on them; they prophesy once.
5. **vv. 26–30**: Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp; Joshua objects; Moses rejoices.
6. **vv. 31–35**: Quail arrive in superabundance; the people gorge; a plague strikes; the place is named Kibroth-hattaavah.
